# Activity partition recipe (v1)

Schema for `.tera/activity-partitions/<name>.hcl` recipes per [ADR-113](../adr/ADR-113-the-activity-partition.md) D1. An **activity partition** is the scope that decides *who may watch a running capability, and who may read what it did*. It is one grantable resource on [ADR-060](../adr/ADR-060-rbac-authorization-model.md) §5's single authorization model, and one topic level of `_sys/v1/activity/v1/<partition>/wo:<id>/inv:<id>` — so the existing ACL engine scopes the live path with no new machinery, and the same value is the top directory level of the session corpus. One grant model on both sides, which is what stops a team's live watchers and its analytical reader drifting apart about what they may see.

**It is declared, and derived from nothing.** Not from the worker — this surface is invocation-bound, and a gateway invocation, a volume sync and a direct call through an exposure have no worker at all. Not from a dispatch input — those are free text nothing validates, so a key drawn from one mints a tenant from a typo and leaves the partition set unbounded and unreviewable. What an invocation is *about* is an attribute a consumer filters on **inside** a partition, never the partition; a deployment wanting finer isolation declares more partitions, which is a reviewed change rather than a side effect of a run's arguments.

**There is no fallback partition and no permissive default.** An invocation resolves to a partition or to none, and none means nothing is stored, nothing is published, and nothing is emitted — the producer is told at start that nobody wants this and never serializes an event. A deployment fronting thousands of short tool calls a second declares no partition on that listener and pays nothing anywhere in the chain: the feature is absent rather than idle. An earlier draft routed undeclared invocations to an operator-only partition; that is a permissive default wearing a conservative hat and it fails [ADR-075](../adr/ADR-075-per-principal-resource-governance.md) D11.

The file stem is the partition value, so `platform.hcl` declares the partition `platform`. The recipe declares a single `activity_partition` block whose label must equal that stem.

## Example

A minimal `activity-partition`: every required attribute, exactly one member of each closed union, and nothing optional beyond what the kind would otherwise render empty. It is generated from the same source these tables are, and the same bytes are run through `tera validate` by the ADR-087 D9 pattern-transfer test — so it cannot describe a shape the loader does not accept.

Cross-references name the other kinds' examples (`example-worker`, `example-tool`, …) because every kind's example is validated together with the rest, as one vault.

`.tera/activity-partitions/example-activity-partition.hcl`:

```hcl
version = "v1"

activity_partition "example-activity-partition" {
  description = "Runs belonging to the platform team."

  retention {
    window = "720h"
  }
}
```

## Attributes

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `version` | string | yes | — | — | const `v1` | Per-recipe grammar version. Required; this schema applies when version is v1. |
| `name` | string | yes | — | — | min length 1 | Bare partition value (the HCL block label), which must equal the filename stem. It IS the partition: a recipe named platform declares the partition that appears as one topic level of _sys/v1/activity/v1/platform/wo:<id>/inv:<id> and as the top directory level of that partition's slice of the session corpus. The loader namespaces the recipe as <vault-id>/activity-partitions/<name>, but the BARE value is what reaches the wire, so the partition namespace is flat across vaults on purpose - two vaults declaring platform.hcl declare one partition, because a topic level does not carry a vault id. IT MUST OCCUPY EXACTLY ONE TOPIC LEVEL, and every shape that cannot is refused OFFLINE at load, so tera validate catches it rather than the first publish. A value containing a slash is refused: the partition is one level, so a separator would shift every level after it one to the right - the ADR-010:294 scope-position hazard, arriving silently, with wo: landing where inv: is read. A value containing a topic wildcard (+ or #) is refused: a partition is a level a producer PUBLISHES to and a grant is written over, not a filter matching several, and a + in the partition position is specifically a request for reach across every partition, which ADR-113 D4 refuses on its face rather than leaving to a later authorization intersection to bound. And a value CARRYING the ACL engine's principal substitution marker anywhere in it is refused - ADR-083 D8's refusal reached one subsystem over. The engine substitutes a whole topic level only and it substitutes in rule patterns rather than in the topic under test, so a partition spelled exactly that way is published to literally and matched by no grant anybody wrote, leaving it permanently and inexplicably empty; and a value that merely contains the marker is substituted nowhere at all, so its grant works and reaches every principal identically. The second is the one an author writes while believing substitution happens, which is why the refusal is on the marker appearing at all rather than on the value being it. And a value BEGINNING WITH AN UNDERSCORE is refused, because the topic grammar reserves that prefix for its own sentinels: _none occupies the Work Order level when a dispatch has no Work Order, which is what keeps ONE subscription pattern total over the gateway case, and a sentinel is a topic level rather than a partition - not declarable, and not grantable as one. The prefix is reserved as a class rather than the one name being special-cased, so the next sentinel the grammar wants does not have to be checked against declarations already in the field. An underscore anywhere but the front is ordinary: team_a is a fine partition. A deployment wanting finer isolation than its partitions give it declares MORE partitions, each one level; it does not nest one. |
| `description` | string | no | — | — | — | Free prose saying what this partition is for and whose runs land in it. Optional, and it earns its place in an otherwise name-only grammar because a partition is a GRANTABLE RESOURCE whose name is the whole of what a reader of an ACL rule otherwise has: platform in a grant says nothing about which dispatches reach it or which team is on the other end of the leak if the grant is wrong. Retention is declared in the separate retention block below, which is off by default: the two knobs answer different questions - one is who, one is how much and for how long - and a deployment wanting live visibility with no corpus is a legitimate posture that a single knob cannot express. |
| `retention` | block | no | — | — | — | Whether, and for how much and how long, this partition's capability sessions are kept on disk as an ADR-114 session corpus - and DECLARING THE BLOCK AT ALL IS THE OPT-IN. A partition with no retention block gets the full ADR-113 live path and writes NO CORPUS BYTES: an operator watching a run of it sees everything, and nothing survives the run. That is the posture PRD-020 section 12 requires be expressible, and it is why retention is a block of its own rather than attributes on the partition - retain everything and let the operator prune is a REJECTED ALTERNATIVE (ADR-114, Alternatives rejected), on the ground that it is the shape that makes the feature a liability by default. An EMPTY block is the other complete statement: retention {} says keep this partition's sessions and take the deployment's defaults, which are keyed to deployment_profile because a single number is wrong in both directions between a laptop and a server (ADR-114 D5). The bounds inside are three because they fail differently and cannot be collapsed - time bounds staleness, bytes bound cost, count bounds a pathological burst - and each is capped by a store-level ceiling so that no partition can declare itself unbounded. Bounds are PER PARTITION and that is what contains a noisy neighbour: a partition can only evict ITSELF, so one team's volume is never another team's outage, which is a stronger guarantee than do not store junk because it holds when the volume is legitimate. Eviction takes the OLDEST WHOLE SESSION and never truncates one in place; nothing expires while the train's root Work Order is live, however long the work takes. What the store actually delivers is MEASURED rather than read back off this declaration (ADR-114 D6): where the byte budget rather than the window is what evicted, a partition configured for ninety days is delivering eleven, and the store reports the oldest session it really holds so an operator and a reader can both see the difference. |

## `retention` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `window` | string | no | — | — | — | How long a session of this partition is kept, as a Go duration string (720h is thirty days). Omitting it takes the deployment default for the resolved deployment_profile - 7 days for embedded, desktop, dev and test; 30 days for server and gateway - because a single number is wrong in both directions between a laptop and a server and the deployment already states which it is (ADR-114 D5). It is a CEILING ON STALENESS rather than a promise of availability: a session may be gone sooner because the byte or count bound bound first, which is exactly the case ADR-114 D6's measured horizon exists to make visible. THE CLOCK HAS TWO SOURCES and neither of them is the session's file. Where the invocation ran under a Work Order the window runs from the train ROOT's terminal transition, as ADR-107 D4 does, so a retry's session outlives nothing that explains it; where there was none - a gateway invocation, a volume sync - it runs from the invocation's own end. NOTHING EXPIRES WHILE THE TRAIN'S ROOT WORK ORDER IS LIVE, however long the work takes, and that rule matters more here than for artifacts because attempt 1's session is what explains attempt 2. A zero or negative duration is refused rather than read as keep nothing or keep forever: the way to keep nothing is to declare no retention block, and there is no spelling for forever. Capped by the store-level ceiling; a longer declaration is clamped to it and said out loud rather than silently honoured. Collection happens between the declared window and that window plus one sweep interval, which is hourly. |
| `max_bytes` | integer | no | — | — | minimum 1 | How many bytes of session files this partition may hold before the oldest whole sessions are evicted to bring it back within the bound. Omitting it takes the deployment default for the resolved deployment_profile - 1 GB for embedded, desktop, dev and test; 10 GB for server and gateway - and WHICHEVER BOUND BINDS FIRST is the one that decides, so on a quiet deployment the clock binds and the bytes never do while on a busy one it is the other way round. EVICTION TAKES THE OLDEST WHOLE SESSION AND NEVER TRUNCATES ONE IN PLACE (ADR-114 D5): a half-evicted session is an incomplete session with no marker, which is precisely what the completeness record exists to prevent, and it would be the one form of incompleteness the store itself caused - so the alternative is refused by ruling rather than left to an implementation. A session whose train root is still live is never evicted for bytes either, so a partition whose LIVE runs alone exceed its budget stays over it and reports a horizon that says so rather than deleting evidence of work in flight. The unit is bytes because that is what a disk runs out of; the total is recomputed by walking the partition at each sweep, since ADR-114 D2 keeps no table to read it from. Capped by the store-level ceiling. |
| `max_sessions` | integer | no | — | — | minimum 1 | How many session files this partition may hold before the oldest whole sessions are evicted. The third bound, and it is not redundant with the other two: time bounds staleness and bytes bound cost, while a count bounds A PATHOLOGICAL BURST - a fault loop minting a million tiny sessions inside one window costs little disk and makes the partition unreadable, which neither of the other bounds notices. Omitting it takes the store-level ceiling, which is a bound rather than an opinion: ADR-114 D5 keys a default to deployment_profile for time and bytes only, and inventing a third profile-keyed number nobody has measured would be a guess wearing a default's clothes. Evicts oldest-whole-session-first on the same terms as max_bytes, and protects a live train's sessions the same way. |
| `sampling_rate` | integer | no | — | — | minimum 1 | Retain one session of this partition in every N (ADR-114 D8). It sits beside the retention bounds and is NOT a fourth one: it decides whether a session is WRITTEN AT ALL, where the bounds decide how long a written one lives - which is the distinction that keeps a sampled-out session ABSENT rather than INCOMPLETE, two things a reader must be able to tell apart because an absent session says nothing about itself while an incomplete one is evidence about the ingest path. It is the answer for a partition whose volume is real and whose value is statistical, so that a busy gateway gets a usable corpus without storing the firehose, and it is the WRONG answer for a partition whose sessions are individually interesting - which is why it is declared rather than defaulted. 1 keeps every session and is the default. The decision is per SESSION and not per event, and it is the same answer for every event of one invocation, so a session is written whole or not at all - a file with holes in it would be an incompleteness no completeness record could explain. Which sessions survive is a function of the invocation id, so lowering a rate keeps every session the higher rate kept and adds more, and raising one loses coverage going forward and never retroactively. The population the sampler refused is recorded per partition per UTC day in the corpus's own census files, beside the sessions, so that a reader computing a rate over what is on disk can scale it by what actually happened: a sampler without that record is a denominator bug shipped deliberately, which is why the two landed in one item (ADR-114 D7). |
